title: Functions
summary: A function is a named group of steps you can use again. It can take values in and give an answer back.
introduction: A function is a named group of steps you can use again. It can take values in and give an answer back. Make a helper that adds two numbers. Call it with different numbers so you do not have to write the same steps each time.
learningObjectives: Declare a function with parameters and call it with arguments
Return a value and explain what a function returns when it has no return
Write function expressions and arrow functions
Explain closures and pass a function to another function as a callback

blocks.text: A **function declaration** starts with the `function` keyword, a name, a list of **parameters** in parentheses and a body in braces. Writing the declaration runs nothing; the body executes only when the function is **called** with parentheses. The values you pass in the call are the **arguments**, and `return` sends a value back to the caller, ending the function immediately.

A parameter that receives no argument is `undefined`. To avoid checking for that by hand, give the parameter a **default value** with `=`; it is used whenever the argument is missing or explicitly `undefined`. A function that finishes without reaching a `return` (or whose `return` has no value) hands back `undefined`, which is a frequent source of 'why is this undefined?' questions.

blocks.title: Printing is not returning
blocks.text: `console.log` shows a value; `return` hands it back. A function that only logs cannot be used in a calculation: `logTwice("hi") + "!"` gives `"undefined!"`. If the caller needs the value, return it and let the caller decide whether to print it.

A function is a value, so it can be stored in a variable. `const square = function (n) {...}` is a **function expression**. The **arrow function** is a shorter form: parameters, then `=>`, then the body. When the body is a single expression the braces and `return` can be dropped, and the value of the expression is returned automatically. Arrow functions are the usual choice for short functions passed to other functions; the [Modern Syntax](/tutorials/javascript/es6-features) lesson covers their other difference, how they treat `this`.

Variables declared inside a function are local: they exist only while the function runs and are invisible outside. A function can, however, read variables from the scope where it was *created*. When an inner function is returned and used later, it still remembers those variables; that combination of a function plus its remembered surroundings is a **closure**. Closures let you keep private state, as the counter below does: `count` cannot be reached from outside, yet every call to the returned function updates it.

Because functions are values, you can pass one to another function, which calls it when appropriate. The passed function is a **callback**. This pattern is everywhere in JavaScript: array methods call your function once per element, `addEventListener` calls it when the user acts, and timers call it later. Note that you pass the function itself (`applyDiscount`), not the result of calling it (`applyDiscount()`).

Function declarations are **hoisted**: the whole function is available before the line where it is written, so you can put helpers at the bottom of a file and call them at the top. Function expressions and arrow functions live in variables, and a `const` cannot be used before its declaration runs.

items: One job per function, named with a verb: `calculateTotal`, `formatDate`, `isValidEmail`.
Prefer returning a value over changing variables outside the function; such **pure** functions are easier to test and reuse.
Keep the parameter list short. If a function needs five settings, pass one object (the [Objects](/tutorials/javascript/objects) lesson shows how).
Default parameters beat checks for `undefined` inside the body.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Write `makeGreeter(greeting)` that returns a function taking a name, so that `const hello = makeGreeter("Hello"); hello("Ada")` gives `"Hello, Ada"`. It is the counter example with a string instead of a number.

questions.question: What does a function return when its body contains no return statement?
questions.explanation: Without an explicit return the call evaluates to undefined. Logging inside the function does not change that.

questions.question: An arrow function whose body is a single expression returns that expression's value without the return keyword.
questions.explanation: That is the implicit return: `(n) => n * 2` returns the value of `n * 2`. As soon as you add braces you need an explicit return.

seo.title: JavaScript Functions – Parameters, Return, Closures
